newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin swallows bitter pill with budget criticism.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin swallows bitter pill with budget criticism.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin looked reality in the face on Friday and declared Russia's 1997 budget unattainable, a bold admission hailed by analysts as one of the Kremlin's first honest assessments of the economy.
The tough talk showed that the 66-year-old Kremlin leader, in fighting mood after months of absence through illness, had swallowed a bitter economic-reality pill.
But analysts said Russia would need more than tough words to get its economy into shape and to meet spending and revenue targets agreed with the International Monetary Fund.
"His words are progress in the right direction but will not lead to drastic changes with drastic consequences," said Russia analyst Catherine MacDougall at Kleinwort Benson in London.
Yeltsin, in a brief radio address, said he had reluctantly signed the budget into law earlier this week to avoid political instability and a collapse in government spending.
But he slammed parliament for making the revenue targets of the document too optimistic.

"There are very major doubts that the budget is capable of being fulfilled," he said, using words analysts said broke new ground in realistically evaluating spending plans affecting everything from foreign loans to political stability at home.
"I am personally very pleased with what he said -- he's a smart man," said one top Russia economist. "He sees that if you got 12 potatoes last year, you'll get only 12 this year."
Russia, its economy battered by five years of market-style reforms, is struggling to fill a chasm of pay arrears which have left many workers and pensioners below the poverty line.

Tax revenues remain vexingly low and the International Monetary Fund, peeved at Moscow's inability to meet ambitious budget targest, said earlier this week it was not yet ready to hand over the latest tranche of a $10 billion three-year loan.
"The government has had problems in the past admitting that the budget it submitted was unrealistic," said one Western economist, referring to budget expenditure and revenue targets.
Analysts said Yeltsin's words were positive.

"This is another step by the Russian government towards honest accounting and it will help its relationship with the IMF," one economist said, adding that cabinet officials had been saying for months that the budget targets were pie in the sky.
One economist said the IMF was working from its own assessment of the economy and looking at the ability of the 1997 budget to meet IMF criteria.
The IMF is still negotiating a 1997 economic programme with Russia. It said earlier this week that release of a $320 million tranche was not on the cards until tax revenues improved.
Yeltsin, out of action with heart trouble and then pneumonia for eight months -- virtually his entire second term so far -- said the decision to sign the budget had been painful.
"I will tell you straight away that such a decision (signing the budget) did not come easily to me," Yeltsin said. "There are major doubts about many key items."
The budget sets a deficit of 3.5 percent of gross domestic product, according to Russian calculations, on revenues of 434 trillion roubles and spending of 529.8 trillion roubles.
Analysts said revenue collections as a percentage of gross domestic product were around 10.5 percent in 1996 and that the 1997 budget targeted an unachievable 16.0 percent.
--Moscow Newsroom, +7095 941 8520 ($1 = 5,676 roubles)
